summary: Changes the checksum used by the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) from Adler-32 to a 32-bit CRC, because Adler-32 detects errors poorly in small packets. It updates RFC 2960. It was later replaced by RFC 4960.

eli5.summary: A checksum is a quick check that a message was not scrambled on the way. The old check missed mistakes in short messages, so this document swaps in a stronger one.

subtitle: Replacing a weak checksum algorithm with a stronger one for better error detection.

tldr.problem: SCTP originally used Adler-32 for error detection, but Adler-32 provides poor coverage of check bits for small packets, raising the chance that transmission errors go undetected.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC replaces Adler-32 with CRC-32c, a stronger checksum algorithm that distributes error detection more evenly across all bits, especially in short messages.
tldr.outcome: The change improves data integrity protection for SCTP traffic. SCTP was later consolidated and clarified in RFC 4960, which supersedes this document.

today: RFC 3309 updates RFC 2960 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 4960, which consolidated and clarified the SCTP specification including the use of CRC-32c checksums.

sections.title: Why Change the Checksum
sections.content:
The Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) originally specified an Adler-32 checksum for detecting transmission errors. However, analysis by Jonathan Stone revealed a fundamental weakness: Adler-32 provides poor coverage of its available check bits for small packets. In particular, for packets under about 128 bytes, the Adler-32 accumulator does not wrap around its 16-bit modulus, causing the checksum values to cluster in a narrow range rather than spread evenly across all possible values.

This non-uniform distribution means that if a transmission error corrupts a small packet, the probability of the resulting packet having a valid checksum is higher than it should be. This is especially problematic for SCTP's first major use case: signaling transport, where most messages are under 128 bytes. The RFC replaces Adler-32 with CRC-32c, a polynomial checksum that provides more uniform error detection coverage across all message sizes.
sections.eli5: Imagine a lock that uses a simple number as its key. For short messages, all the keys happen to be close to the same number, so a random key is more likely to work. CRC-32c scrambles keys better, so a random one almost never works.

sections.title: Checksum Calculation and Verification
sections.content:
When sending an SCTP packet, the sender must fill in the verification tag in the SCTP common header, initialize the checksum field to zero, and then calculate the CRC-32c of the entire packet including the header and all chunks. The calculated checksum is placed in the checksum field. The checksum is computed using the polynomial 0x1EDC6F41 (also written as x^32+x^28+x^27+x^26+x^25+x^23+x^22+x^20+x^19+x^18+x^14+x^13+x^11+x^10+x^9+x^8+x^6+x^0), following the Castagnoli polynomial.

When receiving an SCTP packet, the receiver stores the received checksum value, replaces the checksum field with all zeros, recalculates the CRC-32c over the entire packet, and verifies that the calculated value matches the received value. If the checksums do not match, the receiver must treat the packet as invalid and discard it. The RFC specifies that the CRC computation uses a reflected (or mirrored) bit ordering, where bytes are processed most-significant first but bits within each byte are processed least-significant first. This reflected ordering matches the on-wire bit order for Ethernet and other serial media.
sections.eli5: To send: calculate the checksum on the whole message and write it at the front. To receive: calculate the checksum again on the message, check it matches, and throw away the message if it does not.

sections.title: Why CRC-32c
sections.content:
CRC-32c was chosen over other checksum algorithms for several reasons. The Castagnoli polynomial (0x1EDC6F41) has been mathematically proven to provide excellent error detection properties across all message sizes. Unlike Adler-32, which clusters checksum values for small packets, CRC-32c distributes check bits uniformly regardless of packet length. This means that even for tiny packets under 10 bytes, the algorithm provides strong protection against undetected transmission errors.

The RFC also acknowledges implementation concerns. SCTP implementations could choose CRC-32c implementations based on their design requirements: direct bit-serial hardware for low speed, lookup tables for software on commodity CPUs, or optimized multi-stage techniques for multi-gigabit links. The RFC notes that the bit-reversal or reflected ordering used in CRC-32c computation must be carefully implemented to ensure compatibility across big-endian and little-endian CPU architectures. Sample C code and lookup tables are provided in the appendix to guide implementors.
sections.eli5: CRC-32c is like a special mixing function that works the same no matter what size the message is or which direction the computer's bits go. That makes it reliable everywhere.

sections.title: Security Impact
sections.content:
The RFC notes that the security considerations of RFC 2960 (the original SCTP specification) apply equally to SCTP with the new CRC-32c checksum. The improved error detection does not introduce new security risks. However, the use of CRC-32c instead of Adler-32 does improve the integrity protection of the protocol by reducing the probability that transmission errors or corruption go undetected.

It is important to note that while CRC-32c is much stronger than Adler-32, checksums are not designed to protect against intentional attacks. CRC-32c provides detection of random or accidental bit errors and corruptions during transmission. For cryptographic authentication and protection against intentional modification, SCTP and other protocols use separate mechanisms such as TLS or DTLS.
sections.eli5: The new checksum stops accidental scrambling better than before. But it is not a lock; it does not stop someone trying to deliberately change your message.
